questions.question: How do you monitor and control LLM API costs in a Java production service?
questions.title: Monitoring and Controlling LLM API Costs in Java Production
questions.direct_answer: LLM costs are driven by token usage (input + output tokens per call). Track them via `ChatResponse.getMetadata()` which exposes `Usage` with prompt and completion token counts. Expose these as Micrometer `Counter` metrics pushed to Prometheus/Grafana. Control costs through: token budgets per request via `ChatOptions.withMaxTokens(...)`, prompt caching where supported, model tiering (fast cheap model for simple tasks, larger for complex), and circuit breakers to stop runaway calls. Set cost alerts at the API provider level as a last line of defence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate treats LLM cost as a first-class production concern, not an afterthought
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: No per-request token tracking — discovering cost overruns at the monthly invoice rather than in real-time metrics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss model tiering strategy, prompt caching for repeated context, and how to implement a token budget enforcement layer upstream of the ChatModel call

sections.title: LLM Costs Are Runtime Metrics — Treat Them Like Latency
sections.content:
Unlike a REST API where you pay per HTTP call at a flat rate, LLM APIs charge per token. A prompt that includes a 10,000-word document as context costs orders of magnitude more than a 20-word question. Without per-request token tracking you're flying blind.

Spring AI exposes token usage through `ChatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage()`, which provides prompt tokens, completion tokens, and total tokens for each call. From there the standard path is a Micrometer `Counter` tagged with model name and feature area, pushing to Prometheus and visualised in Grafana with cost-per-1K-token multipliers applied in the dashboard.

sections.title: Token Tracking and Cost Metrics in Spring Boot
Cost Control Levers
sections.content:
**Max tokens cap (`ChatOptions.withMaxTokens`)**
- Hard limit on completion length per call. Fast to implement. May truncate responses — only use where partial answers are acceptable.

**Model tiering**
- Route simple classification or extraction to a fast, cheap model (e.g. GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku). Reserve the powerful model for complex reasoning.
- Implement a `ChatModel` routing wrapper that inspects the request and picks the model.

**Prompt caching**
- Some providers cache repeated prompt prefixes. Structure prompts so the static system context comes first — it's the cacheable part.

**Circuit breaker on cost spikes**
- Wrap LLM calls in a Resilience4j circuit breaker keyed to a Micrometer cost counter. Open the circuit if tokens-per-minute exceeds a threshold.

**API provider budgets**
- Set hard spend limits at the provider dashboard. This is the last line of defence — not a substitute for in-app controls.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`ChatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage()`** gives prompt tokens, completion tokens, and total per call.
- **Micrometer `Counter`** tagged by feature and model turns token counts into observable, alertable metrics.
- **`ChatOptions.withMaxTokens(...)`** caps per-request spend — the cheapest form of cost control.
- **Model tiering** gives the biggest ROI: cheap model for simple tasks, expensive model only where it earns its keep.
- **Prompt caching** reduces cost for repeated context — structure prompts so static content is a cacheable prefix.
- Never rely on provider-level budget alerts alone; detect spikes in-app before the monthly bill arrives.

questions.question: What metrics should you track for LLM-powered Spring Boot services?
questions.title: Key Metrics for LLM-Powered Spring Boot Services
questions.direct_answer: Track five families: **latency** (`Timer` on the full LLM call), **token usage** (`Counter` for prompt and completion tokens), **error rate** (failed calls by error type), **cost** (token counts × per-1K-token price as a derived metric in Grafana), and **quality proxies** (fallback rate, retry rate, empty-response rate). Use Micrometer's `ObservationRegistry` and Spring AI's built-in `ChatModel` observation support to capture latency and metadata automatically. Expose via Spring Boot Actuator's `/actuator/prometheus` endpoint.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that LLM services need a different metrics vocabulary than standard REST services — token cost and quality proxies on top of the usual RED metrics
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only tracking latency — missing token cost, error rates, and quality signals like empty or malformed responses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe how to wire ObservationRegistry into Spring AI for automatic span creation, and how to add custom tags (model name, feature, prompt version) for sliced dashboards

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Latency** — `Timer` on the full LLM call; tag by feature and model name for sliced dashboards.
- **Token usage** — `Counter` for prompt and completion tokens separately; both affect cost.
- **Error rate** — `Counter` by error class (timeout, rate-limit, parse failure).
- **Quality proxies** — empty-response rate, malformed-JSON rate, fallback rate.
- **`ObservationRegistry`** with Spring AI's observation support creates spans automatically — wire it in `application.properties` with `spring.ai.chat.observations.enabled=true`.
- Expose everything via Spring Boot Actuator's `/actuator/prometheus` — same pipeline as your existing services.

seo.metaTitle: LLM Metrics for Spring Boot — Micrometer Counters, Timers, and Observations
seo.metaDescription: What metrics to track for LLM-powered Spring Boot services: latency timers, token counters, error rates, quality proxies, and how to wire Micrometer ObservationRegistry with Spring AI.

familiarity_anchors: RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) are the baseline — LLM adds token cost and quality proxies on top
Micrometer Counter and Timer are the same tools you already use — just with new tags
ObservationRegistry with Spring AI auto-creates spans for ChatModel calls
speakable_v2.standard_example: ObservableChatService wraps ChatModel.call() — Timer for latency, Counter for tokens, Counter for empty responses — all tagged by feature
speakable_v2.hook: An LLM call that returns HTTP 200 with an empty string looks like a success in your existing dashboards. It isn't. LLM services need a different vocabulary.

items: LLM observability is tracking whether calls succeed AND whether they're useful, cheap enough, and fast enough
Standard RED metrics — rate, errors, duration — are necessary but not sufficient
Token cost and quality proxies fill the gap that RED alone misses

beats.text: LLM calls can succeed at the HTTP level but fail at the business level: empty response, malformed JSON, hallucinated answer, or a cost 10x higher than expected. Without purpose-built metrics, these failures are invisible until users complain or the invoice arrives.

groups.heading: Latency — Timer
groups.text: Timer on the full ChatModel.call() — tagged by feature and model. LLM calls are slow (1-30 seconds). P95 and P99 matter more than average here.

groups.heading: Token usage — Counter
groups.text: Separate Counters for prompt tokens and completion tokens, tagged by feature. Prompt tokens are your spend on context. Completion tokens are your spend on answers.

groups.heading: Error rate — Counter
groups.text: Counter by exception class: RateLimitException, TimeoutException, JsonParseException. Error type tells you whether to throttle, retry, or fix the prompt.

groups.heading: Quality proxies — Counter
groups.text: Empty-response rate, malformed-JSON rate, fallback rate. A rising empty-response rate means the model is refusing or struggling with your prompt — not a 5xx, but a real degradation.

groups.heading: ObservationRegistry
groups.text: Spring AI's ChatModel observation support creates spans and timers automatically when ObservationRegistry is wired. Enable with spring.ai.chat.observations.enabled=true.

beats.text: Tag every metric with the feature name ('ticket-classifier', 'code-explainer'). In Grafana, a single dashboard shows cost, latency, and quality per feature. When ticket-classifier's empty-response rate spikes, you know exactly which prompt to fix.

items: Non-obvious: tracking only HTTP status misses empty responses, malformed output, and quality drift
No feature tag on metrics — you can't tell which product feature is expensive or broken
Aggregating prompt and completion token Counters into one — loses the ability to tune prompt length separately from answer length

speakable_v2.cap: Use Timer for latency, Counters for tokens and errors, Counters for quality proxies. Tag everything by feature and model. Wire ObservationRegistry for automatic spans. That's the full LLM observability stack.

questions.question: How do you add distributed tracing to LLM calls using Micrometer and Spring AI?
questions.title: Distributed Tracing for LLM Calls with Micrometer and Spring AI
questions.direct_answer: Spring AI integrates with Micrometer Tracing via `ObservationRegistry`. When Spring AI's observation support is enabled, each `ChatModel.call()` automatically creates a span tagged with model name, token counts, and prompt metadata. These spans propagate through your service's existing trace context (Brave/Zipkin or OpenTelemetry). Add custom attributes via `Observation.createNotStarted(...)` for prompt version, feature name, and token budget. Visualise in Zipkin, Jaeger, or Grafana Tempo.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can extend existing Spring Boot tracing infrastructure to cover LLM calls without reinventing the wheel
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Starting a new trace for each LLM call instead of participating in the existing request trace — loses the causal chain from HTTP request to LLM call to database
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how to propagate trace context to async LLM calls on virtual threads, and how to attach prompt hash and token count as span attributes for cost attribution per trace

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`spring.ai.chat.observations.enabled=true`** auto-creates child spans for every `ChatModel.call()` within the current trace context.
- **`ObservationRegistry`** is the Micrometer abstraction — backed by Brave (Zipkin) or OpenTelemetry (Jaeger, Tempo) transparently.
- **Low-cardinality tags** (feature, model) go in `lowCardinalityKeyValue` — they're indexed and searchable.
- **High-cardinality tags** (token count, request ID) go in `highCardinalityKeyValue` — they're stored per-span but not indexed.
- **Never attach full prompt text in production** without redacting PII — use `include-prompt: false` and attach only a prompt hash.
- Trace context propagates automatically to virtual threads in Java 21+ via Micrometer's context propagation.

seo.metaTitle: Distributed Tracing for LLM Calls — Spring AI and Micrometer Guide
seo.metaDescription: How to add distributed tracing to LLM calls in Spring Boot using Micrometer ObservationRegistry and Spring AI's built-in observation support, with custom span attributes for token cost attribution.

familiarity_anchors: ObservationRegistry is Micrometer's tracing abstraction — works with Brave (Zipkin) and OpenTelemetry (Jaeger, Tempo)
spring.ai.chat.observations.enabled=true auto-creates child spans for ChatModel calls
Low-cardinality tags are indexed; high-cardinality tags (token count) are per-span only
speakable_v2.standard_example: TracedChatService wraps ChatModel.call() in an Observation — feature and model as low-cardinality tags, token count as high-cardinality
speakable_v2.hook: If your LLM call isn't in the same trace as the HTTP request that triggered it, you can't answer 'why was this request slow?' You're debugging blind.

beats.text: Distributed tracing for LLM calls means making each ChatModel.call() a child span inside the current request trace. You can then see the full chain: HTTP request, service logic, LLM call, and response. Timing and token cost show on each span.

Without LLM spans, a slow P99 request is a mystery. With them, you can pin the latency to a specific LLM call. You can see which prompt triggered it and attribute the token cost to the right feature — all from one trace view.

groups.heading: Auto-instrumentation
groups.text: Set spring.ai.chat.observations.enabled=true. Spring AI creates a child span for every ChatModel.call() automatically. No code changes needed for the baseline.

groups.heading: Custom Observation
groups.text: Use Observation.createNotStarted() to wrap the LLM call with extra tags: feature name, model, token count. These become searchable span attributes in Zipkin, Jaeger, or Grafana Tempo.

groups.heading: Cardinality rules
groups.text: Use lowCardinalityKeyValue for model name and feature — few distinct values, safe to index. Use highCardinalityKeyValue for token count and request ID.

groups.heading: PII safety
groups.text: Set include-prompt=false in production. Attach a prompt hash to link traces to prompt versions without exposing user data.

beats.text: In Grafana Tempo, filter traces by feature='ticket-classifier'. You'll see every LLM call for that feature with its token count, latency, and status. One trace view replaces five separate log searches.

items: Sharp edge: creating a new root trace for the LLM call disconnects it from the HTTP request and breaks causal attribution
Using high-cardinality values like prompt text as lowCardinalityKeyValue — explodes the trace index
Enabling include-prompt=true in production without PII redaction — leaks user data into your observability backend

speakable_v2.cap: Enable Spring AI's observation support for automatic LLM spans. Wrap calls in a custom Observation for extra tags. Keep prompt text out of traces in production. Now every slow request tells the full story.
